CHIEF COMPLAINT
Nonhealing foot ulcer

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Gregory presents with a nonhealing right foot ulcer that has been present for approximately two months. He reports that the ulcer recently became red and started draining, which has prompted his visit. He believes he acquired the wound from walking barefoot at Dewey Beach. He describes intermittent throbbing pain but denies specific sharp pain. He reports increased pressure sensation when the area is touched but notes that the redness and drainage are his primary concerns, as he has not experienced these findings before. His primary care physician prescribed antibiotics, but the patient has not yet filled the prescription and cannot recall the specific medication names.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient reports intermittent throbbing in the foot. Denies fever.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Diabetes mellitus

MEDICATIONS
Diabetes medication (patient reports taking but does not regularly monitor blood glucose). Antibiotics prescribed by PCP (not yet obtained).

ALLERGIES
Not documented

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented

SOCIAL HISTORY
Recent recreational activity at Dewey Beach. Patient ambulates barefoot.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Normal, afebrile. Foot examination reveals a one by two inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, proximal to the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint. Erythema, drainage, and edema are present around the wound. No necrosis, odor, or bony exposure noted. Nontender to palpation; patient reports sensation of pressure but no distinct pain.

RESULTS
Right foot X-ray: No evidence of osteomyelitis

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diabetic foot ulcer with clinical signs of infection. Patient's diabetes appears suboptimally controlled with reported A1C approximately 10. Plan includes ordering ankle-brachial index to assess foot blood supply. Wound debridement will be performed to remove necrotic tissue. Clindamycin 400 mg orally twice daily for seven days prescribed for infection treatment. Surgical shoe to be provided for one month to reduce pressure and prevent further irritation. Follow-up appointment in two weeks for reassessment and possible repeat debridement. Patient instructed to call office with any concerns and to seek urgent care or emergency department if fever or signs of systemic infection develop.
